items.title: Edison lost the war of currents in the 1890s
items.claim: Thomas Edison championed direct current (DC) for distributing electricity. George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla pushed alternating current (AC). By 1895 AC had won — and every domestic supply on Earth is now AC for a single decisive technical reason.
items.prompt: Why did AC beat DC for power distribution?

options.text: AC can be stepped up to very high voltage (low current) for long-distance transmission and stepped back down for domestic use using transformers — DC cannot easily be transformed, so it loses huge amounts of energy as heat in distribution cables
DC produces more harmful magnetic fields

items.reveal_title: Power dissipation scales as I squared R
items.reveal:
Power loss in a transmission line is I squared times R. For a given power delivered (P = VI), higher voltage means lower current, and so vastly lower losses. Transformers (Faraday's induction, 1831) require an alternating magnetic flux — AC works, DC does not.

UK grid runs at 50 Hz; US, Mexico, parts of Brazil run at 60 Hz. The choice was historical (early generators in Europe vs America had different design constants) and is now too embedded to change.

High-voltage DC transmission HAS become possible since the 1950s (solid-state converters) and is now used for very long undersea cables. But local distribution to homes is still AC because that's what every appliance and wall socket has been built around.
items.why: AC's dominance is taught as a historical fact. The deeper reason is the I squared R loss in transmission combined with transformers' need for changing flux.

items.title: There is no centrifugal force
items.claim: Swing a bucket on a string in a circle. People say a 'centrifugal force' pulls the water outward, keeping it in the bucket. Inside the rotating bucket-frame, sure. From a stationary frame, that force doesn't exist.
items.prompt: What's actually keeping the water in the spinning bucket?

options.text: Newton's first law — the water 'wants' to travel in a straight line, and the bucket bottom keeps providing a centripetal force inward that bends its path into a circle
Gravity, which spins with the bucket

items.reveal_title: Centrifugal force is a frame-dependent fiction
items.reveal:
In an inertial frame (you watching from outside), the only forces on the water are gravity (down) and the normal force from the bucket bottom (toward the centre of the circle). Combined, they cause the water to follow a circular path — the inward acceleration is v squared over r.

The 'centrifugal' force shows up only when you do physics in the rotating frame of the bucket itself. It's a fictitious force, introduced to make Newton's laws appear to work in a non-inertial frame.

The same logic applies to washing machines, planetary rotation, and amusement-park rides. Real forces always point inward (centripetal) — the apparent outward push is an artefact of trying to use Newtonian mechanics in a rotating coordinate system.
items.why: Everyday language ('the centrifugal force pulled me to the wall') conflates two different physical descriptions. Real forces have specific causes; pseudo-forces are mathematical artefacts of non-inertial frames.

items.title: Sound travels four times faster in water than in air
items.claim: Sound moves at about 343 m/s in air. In water, it moves at about 1480 m/s. In steel, it moves at 5000 m/s. Denser materials slow sound, surely? No — denser is faster, if the stiffness scales properly.
items.prompt: Why is sound faster in steel than in air?

options.text: Sound speed equals the square root of (elastic modulus divided by density); steel's stiffness vastly outweighs its density, giving a much higher ratio than air's
Steel has no gaps between atoms, so sound transmits instantly
Sound in steel uses light to propagate

items.reveal:
Sound is a mechanical wave. Its speed in a medium depends on how much restoring force is generated per unit strain (bulk modulus, K) divided by how massive the displaced material is (density, rho). v equals the square root of K over rho.

Air: K about 1.4 times 10 to the 5 Pa, rho about 1.2 kg per cubic metre. Ratio gives 343 m/s.
Water: K about 2.2 times 10 to the 9 Pa, rho 1000 kg per cubic metre. Ratio gives 1480 m/s.
Steel: K about 1.6 times 10 to the 11 Pa, rho 7800 kg per cubic metre. Ratio gives 5000 m/s.

Density slows things down per unit force; stiffness speeds things up per unit displacement. Steel is much stiffer than air relative to its density.
items.why: Intuition says heavier is harder to move and so slower. The full picture includes how hard the material resists deformation, not just its mass.
